paragraphs: On Saturday morning, the Explorers went to the science museum by bus. Teacher Kim counted the group at the bus stop: Lily, Mia, Leo, May, and May's grandma. Leo carried the green flag with the paw print on it. "Grandma helps us today," said May. "She has never been to a museum." Grandma had a small blue bag, and she held it close with both hands.

At the front door, a receptionist sat behind a long desk. "Good morning," she said. "How many tickets do you need?" "Four children plus two adults," said Teacher Kim. The receptionist looked at Grandma and then at May. "Is May your grandchild?" she asked. "Yes," said Grandma in a quiet way. She did not look at the big hall. She looked at her shoes.

Guide Ann met them at the door with a name card on her shirt. "Welcome," she said. "We start in the Weather Area." Grandma walked slowly along the wall with her bag in front of her. "Do you want to sit down?" asked May. "No, no," said Grandma. "I am looking." Guide Ann gave each child a small card with a question about the weather. Grandma's eyes went from the big clock to the model of the sun and back again.

In the middle of the room, there was a wind machine behind a window. "Put your hand here," said Guide Ann, "and feel the wind." Leo put his hand in the wind, and his hair moved. Grandma put one finger in the wind, and then her whole hand. She put her bag on the floor. "Why does the wind come from this small hole?" she asked. Guide Ann answered, and Grandma asked three more questions. Guide Ann was amazed. "Most visitors ask only one," she said.

Among the four children, Mia whispered to Lily. "Grandma asks more questions than Leo," she said. "That is not true," said Leo, and everybody laughed. Mia took five photos of the sun model for her fact file. Lily wrote in her notebook for the blog. At the end, Grandma took a map of the museum from the desk. "This is a new experience for me," she said. She put the map in her blue bag, and she kept her hand on it all the way home.
